Tech Report: Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.
  • The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security.
  • What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds that the push to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels is accelerating electrification and the shift toward domestic energy sources, including renewables. Yet electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and concerns about energy security are also giving coal a longer life in some countries. The IEA warns that the pursuit of energy security alone won’t deliver the emissions reductions needed to meet global climate goals.

What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts? Nick Wayth, global director of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, explains four key takeaways from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

Q: How close will current and proposed policies get us to the COP31 pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035? What changes are needed to bridge the gap?

The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for electrification as a way for countries to diversify their power sources and reduce dependence on imports, improving energy security and affordability. While the world’s reliance on fossil fuels hasn’t changed substantially, there’s been a real shift in how countries think about the risks of that dependence—and the benefits of electrification. But progress is too slow. The IEA projects that under current and proposed policies, electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035. That’s only half the increase needed to reach the COP31 target of 35%.

Recent findings suggest that much of the technology is already available. The IEA estimates that nearly half of fossil fuel demand in road transport and more than a third of demand for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at a competitive cost today. The challenge is creating the conditions for businesses and households to make that switch.

To reach the target, countries need to develop detailed aims for shifting transport, heating, and heavy industry toward electricity and invest in transmission and distribution. Governments can help keep their industries competitive by making it more attractive for businesses to switch from gas to affordable electricity. Some countries are doing this successfully already. Germany, for example, has reduced electricity taxes for manufacturers and has subsidized grid charges, helping lower electricity costs for businesses.

In a recent development, Q: The IEA projects rapid growth in electricity demand from both air conditioning and data centers. How do the challenges posed by these two sources of demand differ?

It has been revealed that energy demand from AI and data centers has dominated public attention this year, but by 2035 the global growth in electricity demand from cooling is forecast to be about 70% greater than from data centers. Notably, the IEA finds that global demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating them for the first time in history.

Energy demand from data centers is concentrated in the U.S., China, and the EU. By contrast, demand for cooling is widespread, especially in emerging and developing economies where much of the population is vulnerable to extreme heat, an increasing threat to human life.

It has been revealed that under current and proposed government policies, cooling is projected to account for 12% of global electricity consumption by 2035. But during periods of peak demand, when millions of air conditioners are running at once, it could reach around 30% of the electricity needed. Electricity grids must be able to cope with these spikes in demand, even if they occur only occasionally. Without better planning and more efficient cooling, countries could face costly grid upgrades—or risk power outages during extreme heat.

This is why policymakers and utilities need to anticipate future electricity demand and plan investments in grid infrastructure accordingly. But building more isn’t the only solution. Governments and utilities should also invest in energy storage and other grid flexibility measures that enable them to adapt to fluctuating supply and demand as needed.

Q: The energy crisis is accelerating clean electrification in some countries but also encouraging greater reliance on fossil fuels in others. What does the IEA’s outlook tell us about the future of oil, coal, and gas—and the risks of investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure?

The report demonstrates that global oil demand is expected to level off by 2030 under current and proposed policies. The slowdown in China’s oil demand, driven largely by electric vehicle adoption, is expected to continue. Other fast-growing economies, such as India, despite electrifying transport, are nonetheless projected to increase their demand for oil.

The current energy crisis is reinforcing these differences in strategy. Some countries are investing in electrification to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, while others are turning to domestic fossil fuels.

The energy crisis has given coal demand a short-term boost, and the IEA now expects coal use in 2035 to be higher than it projected just a year ago. Even so, under current and proposed government policies, global coal demand is expected to fall by 14% between 2025 and 2035, driven largely by a decline in coal-fired power generation, particularly in China. But coal use in industry is projected to fall by just 5%, highlighting the challenge of reducing dependence on the fuel.

Countries need to be cautious about investing in infrastructure that may not be needed. The IEA estimates that about 400 billion cubic meters (bcm) of fresh liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity is under construction and could come online by 2035. Yet under current and stated government policies, export capacity could significantly exceed demand in 2035 by70 bcm. That surplus raises the risk of underused infrastructure and investments that fail to pay off.

In a recent development, the IEA estimates that the world will need at least 25 million kilometers of fresh power lines over the next decade to meet growing electricity demand and connect new sources of power, including renewables. Another 15 million kilometers of existing lines will need to be upgraded or replaced. Both will require substantial investment.

It has been revealed that the biggest challenge is delivering these changes fast enough. Major grid projects can take 5 to15 years to blueprint, secure permits for, and complete—far longer than many renewable energy projects. Governments need to speed up permitting and grid connections, improve coordination between utilities and developers, and encourage investment before demand materializes. One encouraging example is the EU’s recent provisional agreement to streamline permitting for grid projects.

Equally important is to invest in ways to use existing assets more efficiently. Grid-enhancing technologies can speed up connections by allowing existing power lines to carry more electricity, reducing the need to build fresh infrastructure. And increasingly, governments and utilities are seeing the importance of making grids more flexible—building in capability and strategies to balance supply with demand in real time. Brazil, for example, pays large electricity owners to temporarily reduce consumption when the grid is under strain. Businesses that fail to deliver the agreed reductions can lose payments or face suspension from programs. By combining energy storage, demand-response programs, smart grid controls, distributed energy generation, and other flexibility strategies, energy planners can meet growing demands and increase resilience while reducing the need to build more grid infrastructure.

Industry observers note that courtesy of WRI. By Sarah George, Senior Manager, Strategic Communications, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; and Francisco Boshell, Global Lead, Decarbonized Energy Consumption, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition.

#42160. 7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1593 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans.
  • In a recent development, true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units.
  • According to recent reports, we do have a disclaimer, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans. After all, a motor that size was under the hood of the dearly departed third-generation Dodge Challenger — in which it showed off a horsepower rating well into four-figure territory — and Dodge isn't the only automaker to use a beefy 6.2-liter V8.

In a recent development, true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units. The Hennessey Venom F5, for one, touts 1,817 horses from its 6.6-liter twin-turbo V8. But 6.2-liter V8s, whether they're naturally aspirated, turbocharged, or supercharged, are among some of the most powerful and most well-liked powerplants of all time. We'll get into the details below, but there are all sorts of rides like the Ford F-150 Raptor, the first mid-engine Chevrolet Corvette, the Chevy Camaro ZL-1, and various Mercedes-Benz AMG models ranging from the C 63 to the SLS AMG that use impressive 6.2-liter V8s.

According to recent reports, we do have a disclaimer, though. Engine displacement is generally displayed in cubic liters today, but many automakers do their measuring in terms of cubic centimeters. Then they round up to get to liters. For instance, Dodge's 6.2-liter Hemi V8 actually displaces closer to 6,166 cubic centimeters, so the numbers aren't hyper-precise, but we figure it's close enough.

According to recent reports, the trail-ready Ford F-150 SVT Raptor hit dealerships in 2010 with an optional 6.2-liter unit capped at 400 hp. Ford then made that engine standard, with 411 ponies, the following year. Known by Blue Oval fans and insiders as "the Boss" – though it was unrelated to the V8s of the Boss Mustangs — it could propel the Raptor from zero to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds.

According to recent reports, ford started the engine's development with a goal of producing a so-called Triple Seven – a 7.0-liter V8 capable of 700 hp with a redline of 7,000 rpm. The single example made, many years later, would find its way into a 2005 Ford Mustang dragster that could get through the quarter mile in under 9 seconds. Who knows what kind of numbers the Raptor would have put up if Ford's 7.0-liter ended up under the hood? Even without it, though, the big-power pickup truck was an impressive rig.

For a certain subset of AMG enthusiasts, this is where it all started. The naturally aspirated 6.2-liter M156 V8 was the first motor ever developed from scratch by MB's in-house performance division. All previous AMG vehicles had relied on modified Mercedes-Benz production engines. Of course, many of those engines were built by hand. The Mercedes-AMG philosophy of "one man, one engine" goes back to at least 1976, when the organization had relocated to Affalterbach, Germany.

It has been revealed that as for the first car with the M156, that distinction goes to the 2007 Mercedes-AMG E63, which won Car and Driver's German Sports Sedan Comparo that same year. No doubt impacting the decision, the naturally aspirated engine kicked out a healthy 507 hp and 446 pound-feet of torque. When C&D put that output to the test, the car rolled out to 60 in a mere 4.2 seconds, dispatching the quarter mile in 12.6 seconds at 115 mph. By 2010, the E63's M156 came with 518 hp complemented by 465 lb-ft of torque.

The M156 would end up motivating the likes of the R230 SL 63 AMG, the CLK 63, CL 63, CLS 63, and ML 63, but it's important to note that the "63" attached to these machines was a bit of a misnomer. The M156's displacement remained at 6.2 liters in all these applications.

It has been revealed that the M159 started out with healthy horsepower, and it increased in output over the years. When the car premiered in 2010, its engine could make 563 horsepower, and the AMG SLS GT could serve up 583 horses from 2013-2015.

The 6.2-liter V8 powering the 2020 Mercedes-AMG SLS Black Series made 622 horsepower, which might seem meager by modern supercar standards, but that power output comes from a naturally aspirated mill. What's more, this engine wasn't simply an updated version of the M156 6.2-liter V8. The significant updates ranged from dry-sump lubrication to redesigned camshafts to the kind of lightweight forged pistons needed by some high-performance rides. In all, some 120 of the M159's components were upgraded compared to the M156.

It has been revealed that it's further worth pointing out that Mercedes refers to the engine as having 6.3 liters of displacement. You can chalk that up to marketing, however. To honor Mercedes' first post-war V8, the 6.3-liter M100, the manufacturer decided to also call the M156 a 6.3-liter mill — despite it displacing 6,208 cubic centimeters. That, obviously, should be rounded down to 6.2. Anyways, the naming strategy then carried over to the M159.

Sources indicate that as Chevy's high-performance halo car, it makes sense that the Corvette — especially in its ZR1 variants — has been the showcase for some of the brand's most powerful engines. So we're going to talk about two different versions of the Corvette's 6.2-liter V8: the LT5 from the 2019 ZR1, and the LS9 that came in the 2009 ZR1. First, it's the LS9.

Recent findings suggest that putting out a stout 638 horsepower, the LS9 is part of GM's long-running LS lineup, which is considered a totally different engine generation than the LT roster. One core practical difference is that the former featured port injection and the latter had direct injection, cylinder deactivation, and variable valve timing. Drilling down into the details demonstrates the LS and LT families are set apart by much more than that — there's practically zero parts interchangeability between the two.

Industry observers note that the LS9 proved its performance credibility on the road with zero-to-60 sprints of 3.4 seconds and a top speed of 205 mph. When it debuted, it was Chevy's most powerful production motor.

When Chevrolet ended production of the front-engine Corvette, it sent the car out on top: The 2019 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 debuted as the fastest, most powerful model to ever wear the Crossed Flags badge. Yes, both benchmarks have since been obliterated by the record-setting Corvette ZR1X, but the '19 ZR1 was no slouch. During testing at Car and Driver, the ZR1 covered the quarter mile in 10.7 seconds, reaching 135 mph along the way, and along the way it went from zero to 60 in 2.9 seconds.

According to recent reports, the engine backing those results was Chevy's supercharged 6.2-liter LT5 V8. Now, GM has a tendency to re-use its engine codes, so keep in mind that this is a totally different mill from the 5.7-liter LT5 V8 that Lotus developed for the 1990 ZR-1.

Oh, and the hand-built 2019 LT5 also set a record itself. The LT5's 755 hp and 715 lb-ft represented the most output ever offered in any production Chevy up to that point. Another milestone — the premiere of GM's first dual fuel-injection system — was a key contributor to the output. With that on board, the LT5 had both direct and port injection working for it.

Before it was adapted to be fueled by ethanol and got a huge horsepower bump as a result, the "regular" Demon spent time as the most powerful muscle car in the world. Despite its street-legal status, the Demon was purpose-built for the dragstrip. There, it could make the most of its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 and enter the record books. The Demon tapped into 840 hp to cover the quarter mile in 9.65 seconds at 140 mph, making it the fastest production car in the quarter mile at the time.

The Demon was plenty different from its Hellcat predecessor. To be more specific, while it was technically the same engine, the Demon's V8 shared fewer than 40% of its components with the standard Hellcat. Notable enhancements here extended to a reinforced block with upgraded main caps and deck surfaces, along with a forged alloy crankshaft, forged pistons, and powder-forged connecting rods. Compared to the Demon's 840 hp, the standard Hellcat's 707 hp output seems almost pedestrian.

Dodge first debuted a supercharged 6.2-liter Hemi V8 for the 2015 Challenger SRT Hellcat, setting a template for the increasingly insane Dodge V8s that followed. The basic progression was from the Hellcat to the aforementioned Demon, and eventually to the Demon 170, with each set of changes big enough to count as a different engine.

Consider the 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170. The most powerful muscle car in the world when it released — according to Dodge – this street-legal stunner can spit out 1,250 hp and 945 lb-ft when drinking E85 ethanol fuel. On E10, it still offers up a hefty 900 horses. And although its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 shares its displacement with its predecessors, that's about all it shares. With the exception of the camshaft, just about every internal component on the Demon 170 was changed.

In a recent development, for one thing, to maximize its fluid intake, latest fuel injectors capable of delivering more than 2.7 gallons of fuel per minute were used. On the air side of the fuel-air mixture, the 3.0-liter supercharger benefited from enhancements to its throttle body, pulley, intake valves, valve guides, bearings, connecting rods, and more. The outcome was a machine that could sprint to 60 in an EV-like 1.66 seconds on a race-prepped surface — just as fast as the Rimac Nevera R that set 24 new performance records in 2025.

Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F.
  • In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., spoke at the Milken Institute’s Future of Health Summit last week in Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 attendees gathered at the event, the theme of which was “better health within reach.”.

In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health issues.

Recent findings suggest that when asked about her potential disagreements with Kennedy, Schwartz stated, “I disagree all the time. He’s a lawyer, I’m a lawyer. […] What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He's not someone who just states, ‘No, I don't have room for that.’ He really does value differing opinions.”.

Industry observers note that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, global health officials unveiled just this week. On that concern, Schwartz stressed the importance of supporting CDC’s state partners on awareness, prevention and surveillance efforts.

In a recent development, “MMR is the number one way to prevent measles,” Schwartz mentioned. Today’s outbreaks “happen in communities that are very close-knit communities … that typically do not and have not vaccinated their children,” she said. Most cases are currently among kids over the age of five and adults, according to Schwartz.

Under Schwartz’s leadership, the CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which can face multi-month lags. Schwartz is being investigated by Energy & Commerce Committee Democrats who, during a briefing on CDC’s alleged suppression of the total number of national measles deaths on its dashboard, have called her unresponsive and misleading.

According to recent reports, “As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that 10 people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone,” the Committee leaders wrote (PDF) in a letter on Tuesday. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required.”.

Sources indicate that during her fireside chat, Schwartz acknowledged that "we've lost trust not only externally with the American public, but also internally with the team that works at the CDC,” she said. To address this, Schwartz wants the public to understand that CDC follows the science, is being transparent and “leading with humility.” She pointed to COVID-era “arrogance” from institutions, directing at instead of conversing with the public.

“I want to be a CDC director that really has a conversation with the American public,” Schwartz said.

Internally, the first priority is to add stability to the body, including hiring leaders within the agency so they have a permanent leadership role. The CDC has also created a strategic hiring strategy for 2027 with the input of staff and is looking to its “force extenders” like epidemic intelligence officers and its Public Health Associate Program.

On how she’s planning to work with the latest majority-Democratic Congress, Schwartz noted she was encouraged to see more Congress members coming in with a healthcare background, “who understand how these policies will impact patients.” She said is eager to work with the Congressional Doctors Caucus and to work with both sides of the aisle.

“I know that we may not agree on every matter, but I do think there's a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again,” she said.

One of her priorities for 2027 is having a “21st-century CDC” by bringing innovation into the public health sphere. She called out the Biothreat Radar, a proposed wastewater surveillance program about which she recently spoke with Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey). The program’s proposed (PDF) budget is $52 million. The CDC has also tentatively put out a call for new Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members, which will depend on a final ruling from the appellate court in the agency’s favor.

Recent findings suggest that at the Summit, Schwartz’s comments did not necessarily satisfy some of the attendees. When asked by Fierce Healthcare for his impressions of the interview, a public health worker in the room who did not wish to be named called her a “traitor.".

In his fireside chat closing out the Summit, Secretary Kennedy primarily spoke about food and obesity.

One of HHS' most consequential accomplishments during his tenure, Kennedy noted, has been changing the dietary guidelines to be “science-based.” Earlier this year, the White House released latest federal dietary guidelines, calling for prioritizing quality protein, healthy fats, fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while avoiding highly processed foods and refined carbs.

It has been revealed that the agency is focused on transforming food across a number of sectors, including in Head Start programs—free federal early childhood programs—which have received about $151 million in supplemental HHS awards to strengthen nutrition services. HHS is also focused on rolling out healthy food options in the military, Kennedy stated, and within SNAP by allowing states to request waivers to restrict what SNAP dollars are spent on. As of this summer, HHS has launched a Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, challenging hospitals to put nutrition at the center of patient care. HHS has also encouraged medical schools to increase their number of education hours on nutrition from an average of two to 40 hours, Kennedy said.

“Real” food sales in grocery stores, Kennedy claimed, went up 8% this year, while obesity rates have dropped by 7%. He acknowledged that the drop in obesity rates is more likely due to GLP-1 access rather than healthier eating. “If we can reduce obesity, we can reduce our healthcare costs,” he mentioned, praising Trump’s Most Favored Nation negotiations for lowering the price of drugs like Ozempic.

Industry observers note that “We reward people at every level—the hospitals, the providers, other providers, doctors, insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies—we reward them financially for keeping people sick. And as long as those financial incentives are in place, we are going to be operating a sick-care system rather than a healthcare system,” Kennedy stated. HHS has started to change that by shifting more to value-based care, he added, so stakeholders get paid to keep patients healthy “rather than being paid to keep them sick.”.

Recent findings suggest that when asked what he wants his legacy as Health Secretary to be, Kennedy echoed Schwartz on the idea of following science. “What I want to do is to end corporate capture and the politicization of science … that Americans once again trust the regulatory agencies, they trust the science that’s coming from them,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that he referred to newer guidelines meant to encourage extra transparency from researchers. In 2026, the HHS Scientific Integrity Policy was updated (PDF) to support publishing raw data and code in publicly accessible repositories, preregistering study protocols and transparently reporting all results.

It has been revealed that he said he wants "to make sure that we’re not kowtowing to the food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, all these people who are at the trough taking on the $2.3 trillion that my agency gives out every year. And that instead, that Americans believe that this agency is devoted to their health, that they trust it, and that we are doing the science that we need to find out what is making them sick so that we can all eliminate it as a society.”.

Industry observers note that kennedy's interview at the event did not touch on measles or vaccine policy, where the secretary's policies and communications have garnered broader criticism and controversy than his views on nutrition. Tuesday's announcement that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status garnered a fresh call for Kennedy's resignation among his critics, including the Democratic Doctors Caucus.

Recent findings suggest that also coinciding with Milken's event was the announcement of the inaugural 2027 cohort of the Elevate Investment Initiative. The effort, part of the Milken Institute’s Women Health Network, aims to mobilize $1 billion in net-latest capital for women’s health innovation. The 10 fund managers and companies include Borski Fund, Cross-Border Impact Ventures, Foreground Capital, Meridian Health Ventures, How Women Invest and more. [cut this or move?].

Beverly Hills Penthouse Sells for $21 Million in Enclave’s Most Expensive Condo Deal of the Year

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.
  • After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.
  • Industry observers note that at $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.

After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.

Industry observers note that at $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot. Only 18 condominiums have ever sold for more than $20 million in the city.

Recent findings suggest that "It was a very quick purchase," sales co-agent Amir Ensani of The Fridman Group at The Beverly Hills Estates tells Realtor.com®. The median days on market is 57, according to Realtor.com data.

Ensani says the buyer, a man in the hospitality industry and his family, was—like all of the buyers in the boutique building—downsizing from a local "megaestate.".

In a recent development, "The substantial thing that caught the buyer was a staff of 22 with armed guards," claims the luxury broker. Additionally, the buyer, like many other high-net-worth individuals, was migrating to Beverly Hills in part because it has no so-called "mansion tax.".

In a recent development, enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

Recent findings suggest that the buyer was also a fan of Rosewood Hotels, a global luxury hospitality brand. In Latest York, the firm is behind The Carlyle. It does not have a Los Angeles location.

"It's like a double brand," the agent states about living not only inside of the full service Rosewood Residences but the separately incorporated city of Beverly Hills.

Industry observers note that "A lot of the clients are Rosewood connoisseurs, including this one," he says. "They are accustomed to a level of service that Rosewood provides.".

The Rosewood Residences is the only stand-alone residential complex for the brand in the world, a big plus for the property, indicates the broker.

"A lot of people who love the brand may not want a hotel component, with people coming and going," he states.

Another selling point was that the building is a "pedigree property," built on the site of the former Beverly Hills Friars Club, with interiors designed by Upcoming York-based designer Samuel Amoia.

"He likes to collect pedigree properties," Ensani states of the buyer. "When he saw it, he was like 'I must have it.'".

The three-bedroom, five-full bathroom penthouse blends sculptural furnishings, collectible art, natural materials, and seamless indoor-outdoor living.

It boasts nearly 4,700 square feet indoors and 2,200 square feet of outdoor space with 25-foot private pool and hot tub, as well as a custom skylit floating staircase, a double-sided fireplace in carved stone, and a private rooftop with a spa and an outdoor kitchen.

The penthouse comes with $18,740 in monthly dues (property taxes not included).

With just 17 residences, the boutique building offers plenty of privacy—the penthouse comes with a private four-car garage—as well as security (the aforementioned armed guards).

The amenity suite includes butler service, personalized fitness training, in-residence spa treatments, house car and driver, valet service, and private chefs.

Next year, the building will welcome two Japanese dining concepts, including a steakhouse and an izakaya (Japanese bar and casual dining).

Recent findings suggest that colisting agent Tomer Fridman states the units were designed as "estate alternatives" for affluent buyers accustomed to 30,000-square-foot mansions. (Sally Forster Jones of Forster Jones International & Associates at Compass also headed up sales at the complex.).

"These aren't pieds-à-terre with small galley kitchens," he says. "They were designed specifically for an audience that is accustomed to huge estates.".

It has been revealed that the smallest unit is around 3,200 square feet with around 300 feet of outdoor space, and they top out at 7,200 square feet with 2,400 square feet of outdoor space. Fridman notes it is only one of two condo buildings in Los Angeles with these types of "estate alternative" offerings.

The broker states the generous proportions helped account for the complex's brisk sales, which closed on more more than 50% in presales, a milestone the agency says is unmatched by another LA condominium condo building in the past decade. (The sales team wouldn't say the current percentage of closed sales.).

The estate-like units mean that downsizers can often bring much of their furniture with them—though Penthouse C came fully furnished and curated by the designer himself. Amoia previously designed the architect Robert A.M. Stern building at 520 Park Ave.

It has been revealed that despite the buyers downshifting from sprawling estates, Ensani says there is no singular demographic in the building. "We have families, we have people who are 20, we have people who are 80," he says.

While both agents agree that Los Angeles typically isn't a "condo market,"—with wealthy people historically preferring grand estates on large plots of land—it is becoming one.

Wildfires, the difficulty and expense of procuring insurance, and the expense and challenges of managing staff and maintenance, means that full service condos are becoming much more in demand.

In a recent development, "You have to show buyers that they aren't giving up amenities," notes Ensani. "They are used to sceening and entertainment rooms. You have to show them they are gaining services, and someone else will take care of them for you.".

Penthouse E, which is even larger than Penthouse C, spanning 5,817 interior square feet and 2,442 square feet of private outdoor space, will soon hit the market. The price hasn't been released.

2026 Genesis GV80 Coupe Is An Appeal To Your Heart, Not Your Head

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back.
  • Recent findings suggest that sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6.
  • Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back. And like most crossover coupes, the GV80 Coupe promises to lean more into the sporty side of things than its normal-backed brother. The thing is, it doesn't quite deliver on that.

Recent findings suggest that sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6. It even has bright red seatbelts, but the GV80 Coupe is by no means a sports car. Hell, it's barely sporty and is certainly lacking a bit in the body control area when compared to stuff like the BMW X6 and Mercedes-Benz GLE Coupe. However, if you take the idea of sporty pretentions out of your head, you're in for a much better time, because the GV80 Coupe is a wonderful, delightfully comfortable cruiser with a well-thought-out interior, lots of top-notch luxury gizmos, and practicality that punches far above what you'd expect from a crossover coupe.

Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.

Recent findings suggest that there are two engine options for the GV80 Coupe. A twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that pumps out 375 horsepower comes as standard, but those who aren't lilbabybois can step up to the more powerful (and certainly more interesting) twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that has a 48-volt system with an electric supercharger. This funky motor throws down 409 hp and 405 lb-ft of torque while also getting slightly better gas mileage than the standard motor. Don't worry, it's still not good fuel economy. The EPA rates it at 17 mpg city, 22 mpg highway and 19 mpg combined. It's a thirsty beast, but that's a small price to pay for all of this modest sportiness.

Granted, the GV80 E-SC, fitted with a Genesis-built 8-speed automatic that sends power to all four wheels, can get a move on in a straight line. It'll hit 60 mph from a standstill in 5.2 seconds, according to Car and Driver's testing, which is solid for a 5,132-pound crossover. The GV80 doesn't feel like it's in much of a rush to accelerate, though, and it also lags behind its competition. Without a doubt, it's a smooth powertrain, but it's not exactly sporty — not in the way the red seatbelts would imply.

Recent findings suggest that the lack of sportiness becomes incredibly obvious when hustling the GV80 Coupe around a corner. It's almost as if those seatbelts are red not to denote sportiness, but to show how miffed the car is that I dare push it. The lack of athleticism is evident almost immediately, as the suspension and brakes have a tough time keeping up with the beefy curb weight. There's just too much body roll and not enough steering feel to make for any sort of fun-spirited driving no matter what drive mode I was in, including the E-Supercharged-exclusive Sport+ mode.

What I learned swiftly is that this car really shines as a cruiser. I've mentioned in the past that crossover coupes are the personal luxury coupes of the modern age, and that's true again with the GV80 Coupe. This thing is wonderfully comfortable to eat highway miles in or blast around town as the Ergo Motion driver's seat works on that knot in my back and HMG's wonderful suite of driver-assistance aids keep me in my lane and out of the rear bumper of the car in front of me. The engine, while interesting in its operation, doesn't provide the most inspiring noise, so it's not the end of the world when it shuts up as I drive in quiet, calm luxury through the streets of Newly introduced York.

In a recent development, beyond those lovely quilted leather seats, the interior of the GV80 Coupe is a fantastic place to be that also goes toward its cruising pretensions. Sure, there's some carbon-fiber-look trim, but it doesn't exactly scream sportiness. Neither does the wood, metal, glass, and swaths of suede. Do ya know what that does scream? Nice. Pleasant. Chill. Good.

Another nice, pleasant, chill, and good element of the GV80's interior is its 27-inch OLED touchscreen that serves as both a digital gauge cluster and center infotainment display. Inputs can be made with either fingers or an iDrive-style control knob. I'll admit, the system feels a bit clunky to use the first day or so, a step behind BMW and Mercedes-Benz's latest systems, but after a bit of learning where everything else is, it becomes second nature. Using wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto fixes that problem quickly, too. Adding to the simplicity is the secondary touchscreen below it that has all of the car's climate controls housed within it, and between the two screens is a row of buttons that can pull up core vehicle controls. It's certainly welcome for the Luddites among us.

Sources indicate that aside from the sloping roofline, not too much else was changed on the inside or outside for the Coupe, which isn't a bad thing as the GV80 is a lovely-looking vehicle from the get-go. The GV80 Coupe carries the same 116.3-inch wheelbase as the regular GV80, but overall length increases by an inch to 195.5 inches, and the rakish roofline drops overall height by 0.2 inches. Rear seat occupants probably aren't going to miss the 0.8 inches of headroom they've given up, and if they are ones to complain, ditch them. You don't need that sort of negativity in your life, anyway. You're going to need to trim the fat regardless, because there's no third row in the Coupe.

The GV80 Coupe is no exception when it comes to crossover coupes being a bit silly. No truly practical person would buy one over the normal crossover they're based on simply because they're an exercise in style over substance. They're innately compromised products, and on top of that, they almost always cost more.

A base-base GV80 2.5T RWD starts at $59,195 including destination, but that's not really a fair comparison, so let's look at the GV80 3.5T Advanced AWD — that's the trim level where the Coupe starts from. The regular GV80 in that spec starts at $77,445, while a comparable GV80 Coupe is going to be $83,345. That means you, dear buyer, need to fork over an extra $5,900 for the pleasure of having fewer seats and worse visibility out the rear. I, however, would contend that that is a small price to pay for such a pretty car. Argue with a wall.

It has been revealed that the GV80 I drove was no base-spec, though, as it had the E-Supercharger, boosting its starting price to $89,145. The vehicle's lone option, $650 worth of Bering Blue Paint, brought the final price to $89,795. It's a small price to pay for something that looks this good — it's nearly a concept car for the road, if you ask me. If you think of the GV80 Coupe as a piece of art rather than a car, then it's a hell of a deal, and it's even fairly in line with alternatives from Germany like the Mercedes-Benz GLE450 Coupe ($82,650), Audi Q8 Premium ($78,295), BMW X6 40i xDrive ($78,750) and Porsche Cayenne Coupe ($97,450). It's worth the premium over the latter four based on looks alone.

Of course, if you look at it compared to the normal GV80, things fall apart, but this is a car meant to speak to your heart, not your head. Just take a second to look at the mess your head's gotten you into throughout your life. Perhaps it's time to let your heart make some decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a teen, I loved riding — anything, my skateboard, my bike, whatever had wheels and I could get moving on, I was there for it. Then I spent a few years racing mountain bikes in the NORBA circuit when I was in my mid-20’s. I was never very good — always pretty mediocre, in fact, but I’ll be damned if it wasn’t some of the funnest experiences I’ve ever had. The feel of a trail, the woods, cruising through nature … it’s intoxicating. It always came with a lot of work — mountain biking pre e-bikes was a frikkin workout. Pedaling a bike up a combined 3,000 feet worth of climbing during a race would knock me out for days. If only I was in my teen years or 20s now — LOL.

With bikes like the Yozma IN 11, you can cruise mountain trails at speeds up to 45 mph, and do it completely powered by solar energy, to boot. Compared with noisy, smelly gas bikes, the Yozma can cruise on sunshine and offers the quintessential instant torque of the all-electric motor, making racing competitions with gas bikes an absolute joke — the Yozma will crush them.

Check out the lineup of Yozma bikes here.

The Yozma combines some impressive stats into one good looking dirt bike capable of handling a lot of challenging terrain:.

It also has a number of other features, including wheelie assist, reverse gear and high visibility brake lights.

In a recent development, I think one of the things I’m most floored by is the price. My full suspension mountain bike I used to pedal up hills in the mountains of southwest Virginia as a kid cost about $1500. So does this all-electric dirt bike capable of going 44 mph and helping me do assisted wheelies to impress the ladies. I mean … wtf.

Yozma has an official Amazon store, so you can get yours through that retailer if you like.

HLTH 2026: American Hospital Association, West Health Institute announce new collaboration with BD" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The American Hospital Association (AHA) and West Health Institute declared Tuesday a new collaboration with medtech firm Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD) aimed at accelerating the adoption of technologies shown to improve patient care.

The collaboration builds on the West Health Accelerator at AHA’s Health Research & Educational Trust (HRET), a three-year initiative to aid healthcare organizations in scaling technology-enabled solutions.

“No single organization can close the gap between innovation and everyday care on its own,” remarked Zia Agha, M.D., West Health Institute chief medical officer, in a statement. “This collaboration brings hospital reach, clinical technology expertise and performance intelligence together from the start. We’re beginning with a focused group of hospitals, learning what it takes to make changes last, and building a model that can reach hospitals of every size and resource level.”.

Recent findings suggest that the latest collaboration will begin with an initial cohort of 10 hospitals and health systems. It will incorporate advanced physiologic monitoring with clinical protocols in practice, specifically targeting concerns associated with postoperative complications and longer hospital stays. Additionally, Vizient will provide performance benchmarking and analytic capabilities, the organizations said.

Takeaways from the early cohort will help to identify adoption barriers, refine implementation approaches and outline necessary support to expand the model to a broader group.

BD Advanced Patient Monitoring Worldwide President Tim Patz said in a statement that the manufacturer believes innovation “has the greatest impact when it translates into meaningful improvements in patient care.”.

According to recent reports, “Our experience working with healthcare systems has shown us the value of bringing together advanced hemodynamic monitoring, data and the expertise of hospital care teams to support better-informed patient care,” Patz said. “This collaboration gives us an opportunity to build on that experience, further integrate proven solutions into clinical practice and help more patients benefit from them.”.

#42154. History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2615 w)

History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary.
  • It has been revealed that the upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary. After years of long-shot competition against companies with vastly more significant resources, American Motors Corporation won the Trans-Am championship. The following year, it did it again.

It has been revealed that the upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game. Yet, not long after the metaphorical credits would have rolled following that fairytale ending, the car responsible for those victories would be no more. The car was the AMC Javelin, and by the end of 1974, it was gone.

Recent findings suggest that it's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history. The icons become institutions, celebrated and remixed into anniversary editions, nostalgic ad campaigns, and generations of increasingly expensive collectibles. Everything else is a footnote.

In a recent development, but the Javelin's existence has more to say than the handful of years in which it was made, as its brief run coincided remarkably with a transformative shift in the broader history of the automobile in the United States. It arrived in 1968, when American prosperity seemed limitless, and disappeared just as the country was beginning to confront the limits of that optimism.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, the Javelin became something its creators could have scarcely imagined. Its story is one of ambition, ingenuity, and the kind of underdog triumph that's impossible not to root for. Except, it's also about the difference between reaching a dream and being able to hang onto it.

In the early '60s, the American automobile was clearly becoming more than just a way to get around. The baby boomers were getting old enough to drive, and cars weren't just for families anymore. Women took to the road in increasing numbers, and multi-car households became more common. As a growing market with more disposable income showed an appetite for cars that were more fun and even had a little personality, carmakers were eager to oblige.

According to recent reports, ford led the way. The manufacturer introduced the Mustang at the New York World's Fair on April 17, 1964. The Mustang had a long hood and short rear deck that fundamentally changed the posture of what a fun car could be and started at just $2,368. Available options and configurations could accommodate buyers interested in anything from a free-spirited runabout to a serious performance car.

Recent findings suggest that ford expected to sell 100,000 Mustangs a year. It took 22,000 orders on the first day, and first-year sales exceeded 400,000 cars. The era of the American pony car had arrived, but that meant more than just the Mustang.

Recent findings suggest that plymouth had actually beaten Ford to market with the Barracuda, but Ford gets the credit for turning the segment into a sensation. Chevy answered with the Camaro, Pontiac arrived with the Firebird, and the Mercury-branded Cougar followed its Ford sibling into production.

In a recent development, the pony car offered buyers individuality, excitement, and an invitation to have fun with cars in ways that went beyond simply buying a family sedan with a needlessly-large V8. American Motors didn't have one.

According to recent reports, american Motors Corporation built a reputation around economical, everyday cars since the company was established by a merger of the Nash-Kelvinator Corporation and the Hudson Motor Car Company, which, in 1954, represented the largest merger in United States history. As America embraced the fun, fresh Mustang and its early pony car contemporaries, AMC was struggling with a stodgy and decidedly unexciting reputation.

It has been revealed that enter the 1968 Javelin, a sporty coupe developed under AMC design chief Richard Teague after he had personally advocated for AMC to get in on the pony car segment and start shaking off the buttoned-down, no-fun image. The car had a long hood and daring proportions that clearly made a play at the burgeoning market without being a copy of any that existed so far. In-period advertising called out the Mustang by name, leaning into the rivalry and calling out the Javelin's differentiating features like large, contoured bumpers, hand-finished roof joints, and extra room inside.

Underpinning what some would say is one of the most attractive muscle cars ever forgotten was the basic architecture of AMC's Rambler American, a car that was explicitly built to minimize operating costs and compete with the rise of economical imports. Yet, AMC was able to take the bones of one of the least exciting vehicles on the road at the time and use it as a jumping-off point that could do more than turn heads. Engine choices included a 232-cubic-inch inline-6, 290 and 343 V8s, and, eventually, a 390-cubic-inch V8 producing 315 gross horsepower. A 390-powered Javelin SST tested by Car and Driver reached 60 mph in 6.9 seconds.

In a recent development, people noticed. AMC had first set out to sell just 35,000 Javelins but ended up building more than 50,000 in that first year.

The Mustang might have been leading the herd when it came to pony cars, but AMC wasn't content to spend the Javelin's existence playing catch up and running ads touting its superior headroom or trunk space. Even if the manufacturer couldn't compete with Detroit's marketing or development budgets, it could at least try to out weird the competition.

Recent findings suggest that for 1969, AMC introduced its "Big Bad" paint colors: Big Bad Blue, Big Bad Green, and Big Bad Orange. These were absolutely eye-piercing finishes that came with body-colored bumpers and complementary hardware options like (fake) exhaust shields, stainless steel trim, and a roof-mounted spoiler. Unlike almost everything AMC had produced up until that time, subtlety was not part of the package (and it remains one of the classic coupes that looks sick with window louvers).

According to recent reports, in 1970, the company doubled down, with 100 Javelin SSTs built as replicas of the cars in the Trans-Am racing series, finished in the over-the-top red, white, and blue livery of AMC's competition cars. There was not a unique high-performance engine under the hood, and the replicas came with the same 390-cubic-inch V8 available on the SST. So, aside from a ram-air hood and performance-oriented gearing, this was a car that was all about appearances.

That appearance was spectacular to be sure, though some of those 100 Trans-Am replicas ended up being repainted back into submission, presumably because drivers were getting more attention on the street than they bargained for. All that said, AMC saw that the Javelin had the potential to be a lot more than just a pony car dressed up like a race car. It was headed to the races, and the manufacturer had every intention of winning.

It has been revealed that of course, there's a difference between having the willingness to sell customers a replica race car from the factory and actually competing on the track. Perhaps the likes of Ford and Chevrolet represented immovable racing incumbents, but AMC wasn't going to concede the point.

In a recent development, in 1967, the company commissioned Ronnie Kaplan Engineering to prepare a handful of Javelins for the Sports Car Club of America's Trans-Am series, which included Mustangs and Camaros backed by Substantial Three resources and some of the best drivers in the world. The Javelins were powered by modified versions of AMC's existing V8s, bored out from a factory-stock 290-cubic-inches up to just over 304, but they were still no match for the competition in a straight line.

According to recent reports, despite the horsepower handicap, drivers Pete Revson and George Follmer drove AMC to six second-place finishes and landed third overall in the 1968 manufacturers' championship. It was a promising start, but the team remained a distant third behind the two well-funded factory-backed teams of Chevy and Ford. The following year, Kaplan's team failed to maintain the momentum and the series was roundly dominated by Penske Racing and its driver, Mark Donohue, driving for Chevrolet.

It has been revealed that AMC had demonstrated that it could compete on the racetrack, but the little red, white, and blue Javelin had gone two seasons without a victory. It would have to do something differently if the organization wanted a real shot at beating Ford and Chevy at their own game.

Sources indicate that penske and Donohue were two people who had just spent consecutive racing seasons beating up on AMC and its Javelin, but it turns out that they were also something else: free agents. Fresh off of delivering back-to-back manufacturers' championships for Chevrolet, the pair agreed to revise loyalties and see what they could do with the upstart Javelin. Donohue was anything but a mere hotshot racing driver. He had studied engineering at Brown University, and in addition to being behind the wheel, he was also team manager and chief engineer. Together, Penske and Donohue took to the engineering side of the problem first, starting out by questioning the Javelin's bored-out V8. What if instead of stretching AMC's 290 to the limit, they started with the firm's newer 360 V8, reducing its stroke to meet the series' displacement limit while producing enough horsepower to challenge Chevrolet?

It has been revealed that winning is what happened. Donohue drove the Javelin to the car's first three first-place finishes in 1970, and, for the first time, AMC managed to pick off one of its two substantial factory rivals, pushing past Chevrolet and finishing second behind Ford. The Javelin wasn't just an oddball outsider hoping to deliver the occasional upset to establishment rivals. It was a serious car capable of winning against the best Detroit had to offer.

Of course, while Donohue and Penske were out winning races, AMC also had to continue being a company that makes and sells cars. For 1971, AMC released a substantially redesigned Javelin that was longer, lower, wider, and more visually striking. Bulging front fenders caught the public's eye, not to mention that of Donohue, who appreciated the breathing room the upcoming design would give to race tires on his Trans-Am cars.

It has been revealed that it was here that the AMC AMX shifted from its previous status as its own model in the AMC lineup, becoming a trim package for the up-and-coming Javelin. This new Javelin AMX could then be equipped with AMC's 401-cubic-inch V8, rated at 330 gross horsepower. And yet, somehow, this was just the beginning. The following year, AMC tapped fashion designer Pierre Cardin for an outrageous aesthetic overhaul that included colorful stripes taking over the interior, and, indeed, what was once the most conservative automaker was now creating the wildest muscle car graphics in the business. Along the way it built one of the era's automotive special editions that was truly special.

People were taking notice, including the Alabama State Police, which placed an order for 100 of the 401-powered Javelins for use as cruisers. The Javelin had finally helped AMC shrug off its dull reputation as the manufacturer that brought America the Rambler.

Recent findings suggest that in 1971, American Motors finally reached the goal it'd been chasing since the Javelin started racing. Mark Donohue won seven of that season's 10 Trans-Am races and delivered AMC's first manufacturers' championship. The tech giant that had gotten its start building painfully sensible transportation had finally conquered one of America's most prestigious racing series. The following year, Roy Woods Racing took over the AMC effort, with George Follmer winning four races, becoming the first officially recognized driver's champion of the series, and bringing home the manufacturers' championship for a second time.

After four straight years of throwing the Javelin squarely at the fiercest competition of the day, AMC had done it. But even so, this previously unthinkable victory came at a time when the foundation of the Trans-Am series was beginning to shift. Other manufacturers, Ford and Chevy included, had withdrawn factory support for the Trans-Am series the year before. They were still on the racetrack, but without the intense backing that had pushed the teams forward through previous seasons. Still, AMC was up against some of the fastest cars that the most formidable manufacturers had fielded the previous season, and some of the private teams were anything but amateurs -– it was the private Penske team that brought Chevrolet those back-to-back championships in the first place, after all.

It has been revealed that the Javelin had reached the top. A team of engineers, drivers, and ambitious tech giant people had turned the unlikely descendant of the Rambler into a championship-winning machine. The achievement was nothing short of extraordinary, only it happened just as the mountain was beginning to empty.

The Javelin came of age in an America where the future seemed limitless, with more horsepower, unimaginable freedom, and an endless supply of cheap gasoline to keep it all roaring forward. But while the Javelin was winning car races and AMC was experimenting with wild paint colors plus Pierre Cardin aesthetics, the country itself was starting to feel different.

The Clean Air Act of 1970 introduced ambitious new emissions requirements, effectively tapping the brakes on what made the pony car segment sing. In '73 the oil embargo sent petroleum prices through the roof, and Americans who had never given a thought to a seemingly bottomless supply of oil  were suddenly weighing what they were going to do if gas ran out. The era of giant V8s drinking fuel right from the tap with no concern for tomorrow was coming to an end.

Recent findings suggest that the extraordinary irony for AMC was that the boring, practical reputation it had worked so hard to overcome was exactly what the market was starting to demand. Sensible, economical transportation was back in style, and despite years of running the other direction with the Javelin, the tech giant was well-positioned to capitalize on the shift, with cars like the Gremlin and the Hornet ready to meet the moment. AMC had finally built a performance champion, but its greatest opportunities lay in leaving it behind.

In 1971, the Javelin was taking its victory lap on the national stage. Just three years later, it would be offered for the last time. 1974 marked the end of AMC's unlikely hero, leaving incumbent mainstays like the Mustang, Camaro, and Firebird to carry the segment forward into uncertain times.

It has been revealed that AMC could have stayed in the game, navigating the new landscape as rivals were attempting, but the Javelin would have required significant updates to meet 1975 safety regulations, including an estimated $12 million investment in bumpers alone. The time had come to move on.

In a recent development, that following year, Mark Donohue crashed while practicing for the Austrian Grand Prix. He had seen the potential in AMC's alternative pony car, joining the team to both engineer it into contention and to sit behind the wheel. Donohue died following emergency brain surgery after the wreck, and so 1975 marked the loss of both the Javelin itself and an icon who was central to what it had become.

AMC had done what it set out to do. It had built a car exciting enough for the times, challenged the biggest carmakers in the country, and won it all, twice. Yet, after all that, it would turn out that what America needed just then wasn't a better Mustang after all. It needed a better Rambler.

#42153. How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1465 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.
  • Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.
  • A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

But access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

It has been revealed that the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

It has been revealed that other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

Recent findings suggest that as governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

Sources indicate that national electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

Industry observers note that in 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

Ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

Sources indicate that in the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and initiative grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

It has been revealed that A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

According to recent reports, in Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

Even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

In Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

It has been revealed that in Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they plan and direct investment.

In a recent development, rather than starting with how many upcoming connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

Recent findings suggest that energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Sources indicate that courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat.

Industry News: Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September
