Tech Report: The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.
  • It has been revealed that many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home.
  • Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.

It has been revealed that many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true.

Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.

Industry observers note that these programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable.

First-time homebuyers, often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help.

The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan.

Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment.

While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance, or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses.

In a recent development, here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.).

Recent findings suggest that so, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help.

At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help.

These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look:.

Grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money!

About 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, notes Veronica Khandelwal, vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource, which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch.

“Grants require owner occupancy," she says of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower.".

It has been revealed that forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on.

Deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford.

Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market.

In a recent development, some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal.

Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence.

Here are some of the more popular national options folks might access to help them to pivot from home shopper to homebuyer.

FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase.

FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs.

But buyers beware: The cost of materials and construction labor has spiked since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and work is taking much longer to be completed than ever before.

VA (U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs) loans might be offered directly by the VA or backed by the department. Several factors are considered, such as service history, duty status, income, and credit rating. But those who qualify can purchase a home with zero down as long as the sales price isn’t higher than the home’s appraised value.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are federally funded loans that can help buyers skirt steep down payments. The Home Possible, HomeReady, and HomeOne loans typically offer a 3% down payment mortgage to qualifying, lower-income homebuyers.

It has been revealed that good Neighbor Next Door is another HUD-sponsored program. In this case, law enforcement officers, teachers, firefighters, and emergency medical technicians can enjoy a substantial incentive in the form of a discount of 50% from the list price of the home in a community that is being revitalized. The buyer must live in the house for three years as a primary residence.

Industry observers note that teacher Next Door Grant is a program similar to the one above but is designed to help educators own their own homes. Grants to the tune of up to $8,000 in certain areas are possible with additional down payment assistance available in some circumstances.

The USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) Rural Home Loan Program was created to assist people buying homes in rural locations. For qualifying, single-family properties, loans might be available with no money down. There are maximum income limits and other qualifications to be eligible for one of these mortgages.

There are plenty of other programs available as well. Different states and cities, as well as individual lenders and nonprofits, can help prospective homebuyers get the financing they need. Folks should put their location and "down payment assistance" into a search engine, and take a look at what's available. They might see everything from Habitat for Humanity to local religious organizations pop up. Also,visit Down Payment Resource.

According to recent reports, one other path to explore is whether a buyer's job provides down payment assistance. A lot of employers may offer assistance in  the form of a $10,000 loan that is forgivable after five years.

According to recent reports, down payments hit a four-year low at the start of 2026. The median payment fell to $23,400 and 12.8% in Q1 2026, down 19% and 1.2 ppts year over year.

However, down payments remain well above pre-pandemic levels, as more buying is happening in the lower-down-payment South and Midwest, even as the Northeast stays deeply competitive.

The Northeast posted the highest median down payment at $57,600, reflecting higher home prices and more competition. The Northeast also sees the largest gap between what buyers are paying as a down payment today compared to pre-pandemic.

It has been revealed that compared to 2019, the Northeast has seen down payments climb 236.8%, significantly more than the next closest gap of 134.0% in the Midwest. These trends are consistent with the persistent upward pressure on home prices in these regions as scarce inventory is met with sustained buyer demand.

It has been revealed that get ready for some good news. There are a lot of misconceptions about who qualifies for down payment assistance.

“Many people think these programs are only available to low-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers, or for properties that have sales price limits,” says Down Payment Resource's Khandelwal. “But if you look, you’ll find specialized programs designed to assist specific groups, including first-generation homebuyers, minorities, Indigenous people, people of color, veterans, those with government jobs, disabilities, and more.”.

Here’s something else to smile about: A first-time homebuyer doesn't just mean someone who's never bought a home before.

Sources indicate that the federal government generally holds a broader definition of a first-time homebuyer. It’s someone who has not been a homeowner in the past three years. If you sold a house three-and-a-half years ago, you qualify as first-time buyer.

Buyers can take several different steps to find a down payment assistance program that’s right for them.

Check the federal programs mentioned above (like HUD, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac), and see if there’s anything suitable.

Sources indicate that buyers should also visit their state’s Department of Housing website and see what might be listed, or call their number and inquire what down payment assistance programs might be available. Cities, towns, private lenders, and nonprofits may also have help.

“Homebuyers should seek the assistance of a mortgage lender who specializes in affordable lending to identify their best options,” advises Khandelwal.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of what is typically needed to access aid, the documentation is very much in line with what’s needed to apply for any mortgage. Buyers will likely need the following:.

Pay stubs plus W-2s from the past few years to verify employment and income history.

Any 1099 forms showing other income.

Details on the property they intend to buy (The real estate agent can share this information.).

The paperwork is processed in much the same way as a home loan, and there may be requests for more documents.

Then, if buyers are approved, they will be ready to move ahead with a lower—or no—down payment as their homeownership journey unfolds.

Janet Siroto is a journalist, editor, and trend tracker. Her work has appeared in Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping, and other publications.

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

In a recent development, the partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

Ibrahim said that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very big mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim mentioned.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

According to recent reports, “It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”.

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”.

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim noted frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

Recent findings suggest that “I think that would be a huge milestone,” he said. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”.

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim noted he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he remarked.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its upcoming partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it.
  • The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training.
  • To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating upcoming bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health.

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," stated Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits.

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, indicated no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter.

In a recent development, the results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Recent findings suggest that rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming upcoming bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially notable for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a newly introduced activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

In a recent development, the findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

In a recent development, the U.S. Department of Labor proposed new policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Industry observers note that right now, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

In a recent development, the exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, said it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations currently listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”.

It cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now states it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

Sources indicate that “The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”.

It has been revealed that the proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor remarked.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

Among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elle and Dakota Fanning have been in the spotlight for decades, but their upcoming project, “The Nightingale,” marks the first time they’ve played sisters onscreen—an experience that brought them “closer” together, both on set and at home.

While they’ve visited each other on set in the past and even separately played different versions of the same character in the 2001 film “I Am Sam,” Elle, 28, told Vanity Fair that actually working with each other is a totally different ball game.

“It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer,” she mentioned. “Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”.

Dakota, 32, confirmed that they took their mother’s advice.

“We did really savor it,” she said. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything. That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”.

Recent findings suggest that that said, the job wasn’t easy. The Fannings traveled to Budapest to shoot on location, where they lived together.

“It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” said Elle.

After a long day of using lots of “brain power” on set, the sisters had to find a way to “recharge” each evening.

For Dakota and Elle, that meant eating lots of Thai food and streaming “The Real Housewives,” true crime, and “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”—the TV series the younger sister stars in, which was released while they filmed “The Nightingale.”.

Dakota revealed that on a day off, she’d often find herself cleaning up after Elle, which was poetic as her character, Vianne, also tidies her sister Isabelle’s mess.

Sources indicate that “Her bed in the mornings is like a tornado has run through it,” she noted. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”.

The older sister mentioned that “it became a routine,” and she “always made her bed like that” when possible.

Elle noted, “It’s art imitating life, because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed, too.”.

Dakota and Elle were born in Conyers, GA. As young girls, they traveled between the Atlanta suburb and Los Angeles to work before relocating to the West Coast full time.

It has been revealed that “When we were younger, we wanted to make sure that people saw us differently, and we wanted to give each other space to carve our own path,” Elle told Vanity Fair in 2025. “But as adults, it’s been very fulfilling to merge.”.

One of the most major ways the sisters have merged their lives in adulthood was in 2017, when they purchased a gorgeous $2.3 million property together.

According to Architectural Digest, they lived in a Cape Cod-style home in the Valley Village area of San Fernando Valley.

The 4,550-square-foot residence was perched at the end of a private, gated driveway and had a very classic aesthetic with white rose bushes planted along the front walkway.

The interiors were defined by delicate details, such as baby blue brocade-patterned walls, intricate chandeliers, and coffered ceilings.

The sisters sold the six-bedroom, six-bathroom estate for just under $2.7 million in May 2020.

It’s clear that Dakota was a fan of the dwelling’s traditional style, as she bought a very similar-looking home in Toluca Lake for $2.95 million in 2019, just before offloading the property she shared with Elle.

It has been revealed that according to Architectural Digest, Dakota’s newer home spans 4,428 square feet and boasts five bedrooms and six bathrooms. It’s flooded with natural light and, like the first home, has crystal chandeliers, a pool in the backyard, and a double-height entry hall.

Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. Upcoming research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy mentioned. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The latest analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Industry observers note that murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

Recent findings suggest that "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

Industry observers note that the research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," remarked Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

Industry observers note that the growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

Industry observers note that this increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

Industry observers note that "There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy noted. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

In a recent development, murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

It has been revealed that the researchers then initiative to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce notable features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as upcoming registry information becomes available each year.

Recent findings suggest that murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Industry observers note that current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

Sources indicate that she also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

Study Funding and Future Cancer Research.

It has been revealed that the research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Sources indicate that along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, newly introduced cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a new program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant stated Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

Sources indicate that the program is right now available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company noted, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

Recent findings suggest that “Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” mentioned Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This new model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”.

UHC noted that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

In a recent development, for example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark remarked the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she said.

#42085. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • It has been revealed that the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • Sources indicate that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

It has been revealed that the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Sources indicate that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

According to recent reports, between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

Sources indicate that the researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Industry observers note that meat protein highlighted a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

What the Findings Mean for Men's Health.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

Recent findings suggest that "Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," indicates Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

It has been revealed that an notable limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four months after announcing their split, “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” cast member Angie Katsanevas and her estranged husband, Shawn Trujillo, are now living in separate homes.
  • “Recently, Shawn has bought a place that’s two minutes down the street.
  • In a recent development, according to a Page Six report, Trujillo's new pad is a $1.1 million condo he purchased in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four months after announcing their split, “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” cast member Angie Katsanevas and her estranged husband, Shawn Trujillo, are now living in separate homes.

“Recently, Shawn has bought a place that’s two minutes down the street. And I’m at home with Elektra,” Katsanevas revealed in a upcoming People magazine interview.

In a recent development, according to a Page Six report, Trujillo's new pad is a $1.1 million condo he purchased in September. The two-story dwelling spans 2,568 square feet and includes three bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

The couple, who married in June 1999, have yet to legally divorce, but are "moving toward" that status.

“We are separated. We haven’t put it on paper, but we are not reconciling as far as staying married,” the reality TV star, 53, explained. “I hate the massive D-word, but I’ll just have to say that, yeah, we are moving toward the big D.”.

The salon owner’s home—which viewers will recognize from the reality series—is a sprawling hillside estate that has been on and off the market for the past two years.

Recent findings suggest that the four-bedroom, three-bathroom modern abode was first listed for $4.5 million in September 2024. The price was decreased to $4.38 million in March 2025, then to $3.85 million just two months later.

By December of last year, the listing was removed. It hit the market again in January 2026 for $3.85 million, where it sat for most of the year before being removed on Oct. 14.

Recent findings suggest that the couple purchased the 6,369-square-foot residence for an undisclosed sum in 2020. With soaring ceilings, white ash floors, and lots of sleek, marble surfaces, the modern abode has a distinct luxurious aesthetic.

The home has two primary suites, with one that includes a fireplace, sitting area, and double-vanity bathroom with a striking view of the surrounding Utah landscape. There are also dual walk-in closets.

The second is located on the main floor and also has two-walk in closets and a gorgeous bathroom.

According to recent reports, features in pairs seem to be a feature of the home in general, as there are also two kitchens. In addition to the chic white minimalist space at the center of the home, a concealed catering kitchen is equipped with Miele appliances, a separate refrigerator and freezer, and a space for staff to prepare food.

It seems as if, despite the separation, daily life hasn’t changed too much in the home. Katsanevas noted that Trujillo stops by most days to pick up their 15-year-old daughter, Elektra, and take her to school.

According to recent reports, “He’ll come in and have coffee,” she explained. “He’ll bring her home from lessons, and we’ll have dinner together. We are still just spending time together. We’re best friends. We are peaceful, it’s positive. We have a lot to do together.”.

She noted that Trujillo remains close with her father and will celebrate the holidays with the family.

“My dad sends him all of his favorite dishes and continues to cook for him,” said Katsanevas. “Shawn will spend Thanksgiving and Christmas with my family.”.

Although they are still connected in many ways, Katsanevas noted that after nearly three decades together, “space and doing things independently” have brought clarity.

According to recent reports, “We are even going to different churches now,” she shared. “And that’s huge for me. We started out going to the same church.”.

Katsanevas also shut down rumors that she had initiated the split over their opposing political stances, a rumor that started after she cited their “different views” in a confessional interview during a recent episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”.

Sources indicate that “I’m not throwing a 30-year marriage away because of rumors or political views,” she stated. “There are so many things that Shawn and I have grown apart and have different views on, a lot of things at this stage of life. And it’s not one thing. It’s just, we’re very different people.”.

They’re still business partners, however, and are set to open a latest hair salon together in Miami.

“We are continuing to grow our brand together, even though we are separated,” she said.

Katsanevas and Trujillo currently operate nine locations of their business, Lunatic Fringe Salon, across Utah, Ohio, and Idaho.

While she’s focused on remaining positive, Katsanevas said it took some time to work through the complicated feelings that accompanied the change.

Recent findings suggest that “It does take a minute to mourn the loss of the way your life once was and what it looked like,” she mentioned. “I’ve processed, I’ve cried, I’ve accepted. I’ve had to swim away from the muddy waters to get to the clear water and say, ‘OK, I’m coming out of this and I’m going to be OK.’”.

Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Aetna is rolling out a upcoming program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

Industry observers note that the offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access problem, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Industry observers note that aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she said.

In a recent development, aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she stated.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz stated the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.

#42079. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to latest research from the University of Tübingen.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to latest research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

It has been revealed that the birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results revealed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

Recent findings suggest that the team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an notable role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as swiftly as primates.

It has been revealed that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

In a recent development, greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert states, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the fresh place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the newly introduced address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

In a recent development, even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your newly introduced home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

According to recent reports, as you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

Industry observers note that one of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the tech giant’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

Industry observers note that the Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The firm sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.

In a recent development, san Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

Industry observers note that the aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's new valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are Newly introduced York City, at $3.26 trillion, and Los Angeles, at $2.64 trillion.

Furthermore, the AI giant’s valuation tops the owner-occupied home value in 46 out of the 50 states, as well as Washington, DC.

The value of all owner-occupied homes in the state of Latest Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just shy of Anthropic’s valuation.

According to recent reports, throughout the country, all owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion. Anthropic’s valuation equals about 3.4% of all owner-occupied housing wealth in the United States.

When it comes to homes on the market, Anthropic’s valuation stacks up high.

Across the U.S., about 1.18 million homes are for sale, listed for a combined $816 billion. Anthropic’s valuation could snap up every single one and still have $678 billion left.

Even without the first $1 trillion of the valuation, the remaining $494 billion could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listing value with billions to spare: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion.

As Anthropic’s debut is discussed, the valuation may be rounded to $1.49 trillion, as it’s common for financial figures to be kept to one or two digits. However, that dropped digit in the $1.494 trillion figure is $4 billion. That rounding error alone is greater than the combined value of every owner-occupied home in Racine, WI, which total $3.97 billion.

Industry observers note that that same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska: 2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion. For a change in scenery, it could then cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market, which has 356 listings worth $925 million, and still have about $1.9 billion left to purchase all the homes for sale in the Boulder, CO, metro area.

It’s no wonder the AI boom is reshaping markets in tech hubs like Latest York City and San Francisco, when the valuation of just one company looms so high.
